claims.evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the data in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 95.1% of genes in the library are of human origin, and the rest are of mouse or rat origins.
claims.source: 95.1% of genes in the library are of human origin, and the rest are of mouse or rat origins (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: 46.8% of clones have Flag tag, 46.5% have tandem HA/Flag tags, 3.4% have HA tag, 2.4% have Myc tag, and 0.9% have GFP tag.
claims.source: All clones are epitope-tagged, with 46.8% in Flag tag, 46.5% in tandem HA/Flag tags, 3.4% in HA tag, 2.4% in Myc tag, and 0.9% in GFP tag.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: 54.7% of the clones have epitope tags on the N-terminal, and 45.3% of clones are tagged on the C-terminal.
claims.source: 54.7% of the clones have epitope tags on the amino (N)-terminal, and 45.3% of clones are tagged on the carboxyl (C)-terminal (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: 37% of plasmids showed high level of expression, 58.5% had medium or low expression, and 4.5% could not be detected.
claims.source: By western blotting, 37% of plasmids showed high level of expression, 58.5% had medium or low expression, and 4.5% could not be detected (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the western blotting data summarized in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A total of 456 kinases were annotated, while the other 8 kinases were not detected.
claims.source: A total of 456 kinases were annotated, while the other 8 kinases were not detected.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the imaging screen.

claims.claim: About 50.2% of the kinome mainly localized in the cytosol, followed by 16.4% in nucleus, and 10.3% on plasma membrane.
claims.source: In the initial screen, about 50.2% of the kinome mainly localized in the cytosol, followed by 16.4% in nucleus, and 10.3% on plasma membrane (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: 77.5% of the STE family were in cytosol, significantly higher than other families.
claims.source: 77.5% of the STE (homologues of yeast Ste7, Ste11, and Ste20 kinases) family were in cytosol, significantly higher than other families (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: CMGC, atypical, and CAMK families were more enriched for nuclear kinases, 39.0, 34.5, and 30.2%, respectively.
claims.source: On the other hand, CMGC (CDK, MAPK, GSK3, and CLK kinases), atypical, and calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinases (CAMK) families were more enriched for nuclear kinases, 39.0, 34.5, and 30.2%, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of family distributions.

claims.claim: The TK family was enriched for kinases on the plasma membrane, largely due to the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) subfamily.
claims.source: The TK family was enriched for kinases on the plasma membrane, largely due to the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) subfamily.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and is consistent with known biology of RTKs.

claims.claim: The AGC family was overrepresented on the plasma membrane reflecting their functions in relaying extracellular signals.
claims.source: The AGC (family of protein kinases A, G, and C) family was also overrepresented on the plasma membrane reflecting their functions in relaying extracellular signals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data and known functions of AGC kinases.

claims.claim: Most mitochondrial kinases were in the atypical kinase family.
claims.source: Most mitochondrial kinases were in the atypical kinase family.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of family distributions.

claims.claim: The RGC and PKL families were largely formed by ER- and Golgi-localized kinases.
claims.source: Finally, the receptor guanylate cyclase (RGC) and PKL families were largely formed by ER- and Golgi-localized kinases.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of family distributions.

claims.claim: KA annotated 18 kinases on top of COMPARTMENTS and HPA.
claims.source: 6 kinases were not covered by any of the three resources, and KA annotated 18 kinases on top of COMPARTMENTS and HPA (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Six kinases were annotated for the first time: STK32C, SBK2, STKLD1, TSSK1B, NME8, and SRPK3, which were all cytosolic in KA.
claims.source: Manual literature search eliminated 12 kinases with at least one report, resulting in 6 kinases annotated for the first time, including STK32C, SBK2, STKLD1, TSSK1B, NME8, and SRPK3, which were all cytosolic in KA (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by literature search and the imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: 71.2% of kinases documented by both KA and COMPARTMENTS matched with one of the high-confidence localizations in COMPARTMENTS.
claims.source: Among 337 kinases documented by both KA and COMPARTMENTS, 71.2% matched with one of the high-confidence localizations in COMPARTMENTS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: 74.8% of localizations were consistent between revised KA and COMPARTMENTS.
claims.source: Comparison between revised KA and COMPARTMENTS revealed 74.8% localizations were consistent (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: KA uniquely annotated 103 kinase localizations different from other databases.
claims.source: Furthermore, KA uniquely annotated 103 kinase localizations different from other databases (Supplementary file 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: These unique localizations were largely unpredictable by mainstream subcellular localization prediction tools such as WoLF PSORT and YLoc.
claims.source: Importantly, these localization were largely unpredictable by main stream subcellular localization prediction tools such as WoLF PSORT and YLoc (Briesemeister et al., 2010; Horton et al., 2007; Figure 2H and Supplementary file 6), suggesting new localization mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the prediction analysis shown in Figure 2H and citations to the prediction tools.

claims.claim: Seven kinases exhibited novel plasma membrane localization in KA: RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, NLK, MAPK11, and FRK.
claims.source: Seven kinases exhibited novel plasma membrane localization in KA (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the imaging data in Figure 3A and fractionation data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, and NLK were mainly membranous, while MAPK11 and FRK were partially in membrane fractions.
claims.source: Cellular fraction confirmed that RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, and NLK were mainly membranous, while MAPK11 and FRK were partially in membrane fractions (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the fractionation data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: POMK has an ER-related function in phosphorylating glycosylation-specific O-mannose and is mutated in dystroglycanopathies.
claims.source: POMK has an ER-related function in phosphorylating glycosylation-specific O-mannose and is mutated in a neuromuscular disorder dystroglycanopathies (Di Costanzo et al., 2014; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Costanzo et al., 2014 and Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claims.claim: POMK localizes to the ER.
claims.source: By co-expression with GFP-tagged SEC61B, an ER resident protein, we confirmed the ER localization of POMK (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the co-localization data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: SGK3 was enriched in vesicles around the Golgi, with lower expression in the Golgi itself.
claims.source: SGK3 was enriched in vesicles around the Golgi, with lower expression in the Golgi itself (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: SGK3 colocalized with endosomal marker EEA1.
claims.source: In addition, SGK3 colocalized with endosomal marker EEA1 as previously reported (Xu et al., 2001; Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the co-localization data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Xu et al., 2001.

claims.claim: SGK3 is secreted to the extracellular space.
claims.source: Interestingly, SGK3, but not other kinases examined, could be immunoprecipitated from culture medium (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating it was secreted, although at a much lower level than FAM20C.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation data from culture medium shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: SGK3 secretion is not blocked by brefeldin A.
claims.source: First, treatment of cells with brefeldin A (BFA), an inhibitor of ER/Golgi‐trafficking (Misumi et al., 1986), blocked secretion of FAM20C, but not SGK3 (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the BFA treatment data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Misumi et al., 1986.

claims.claim: SGK3 is enriched in exosomes.
claims.source: Second, when exosomes were sedimented from medium by ultracentrifugation, SGK3 but not FAM20C was enriched in the pellet fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: SGK3 is a new exosomal kinase.
claims.source: Thus, SGK3 is a new exosomal kinase, which may mediate cellular communication with the microenvironment.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing SGK3 in exosomes.

claims.claim: MAP4K3 localizes to tubule-like structures that colocalize with microtubules and ER.
claims.source: We found MAP4K3 in tubule-like structures in KA. Co-staining indicated that MAP4K3 structures were colocalizing with a small fraction of microtubules (Figure 3F). These tubules were also non-overlapping with lysosomes even in amino acid starvation condition or in cells treated with vacuolin-1, a chemical that cause lysosome fusion and enlargement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). However, MAP4K3 tubules were overlapping with ER (Figure 3F), which was confirmed by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the co-staining data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: MAP4K3 tubules are obvious in A549, Du 145, and H460 cells, all of which have mutation of the LKB1 gene.
claims.source: Interestingly, MAP4K3 tubules were also obvious in A549, Du 145, and H460 cells, all of which, as well as HeLa cells, have mutation of the LKB1 gene, an upstream regulator of mTOR (Corradetti et al., 2004; Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3H and citation to Corradetti et al., 2004.

claims.claim: MAP4K3 is mainly cytoplasmic with some small puncta in LKB1-wildtype COS-7, U-2 OS, and MCF10A cells.
claims.source: Surprisingly, MAP4K3 were mainly cytoplasmic with some small puncta in LKB1-wildtype COS-7, U-2 OS, and MCF10A cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Restoration of LKB1 expression in H460 cells markedly inhibited MAP4K3 tubules.
claims.source: Furthermore, restoration of LKB1 expression in H460 cells markedly inhibited MAP4K3 tubules (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: VRK3, BRD3, CDK8, CDKL3, TRIM24, and RPS6KA4 were enriched in periphery regions of the nucleus.
claims.source: For instance, TRIB1, CDK10, CDK7, HASPIN, and STK17A were evenly distributed in nucleoplasm, while VRK3, BRD3, CDK8, CDKL3, TRIM24, and RPS6KA4 were enriched in periphery regions of the nucleus (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: All six nuclear peripheral kinases were found within the nuclear boundary.
claims.source: By high-resolution microscopy, all six nuclear peripheral kinases were found within the nuclear boundary (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: VRK3 phosphorylated nuclear envelope protein barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF), thus played a role in cell cycle regulation.
claims.source: Interestingly, it was reported that VRK3 phosphorylated nuclear envelope protein barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF), thus played a role in cell cycle regulation (Park et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2015.

claims.claim: CDK13 and STK19 were found in structures reminiscent of nucleoli.
claims.source: Two kinases CDK13 and STK19 were found in structures reminiscent of nucleoli (Figure 4A), which was confirmed by co-staining with a nucleolar protein UTP25 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting their potential roles in ribosome biogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4A and co-staining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Nuclear puncta formed by TRIB3 and HIPK2, as well as cytoplasmic puncta of BMP2K and CIT were largely eliminated by 1,6-hexanediol.
claims.source: Nuclear puncta formed by TRIB3 and HIPK2, as well as cytoplasmic puncta of BMP2K and CIT were largely eliminated by Hex (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the hexanediol treatment data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Time-lapse live-cell imaging revealed frequent puncta movements and fusion events for TRIB3, HIPK2, and BMP2K.
claims.source: Time-lapse live-cell imaging revealed frequent puncta movements and fusion events for TRIB3, HIPK2, and BMP2K, demonstrating their dynamic and liquid-like properties (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: HIPK2 and BMP2K have prion-like regions overlapping with IDRs.
claims.source: Importantly, among all kinases analyzed, HIPK2, and BMP2K uniquely have prion-like regions overlapping with IDRs, which are largely devoid of charged residues, but enriched for polar residues, and are frequently involved in LLPS (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Deletion of IDRs eliminated puncta of TRIB3 and BMP2K.
claims.source: Furthermore, deletion of IDRs eliminated puncta of TRIB3 and BMP2K, supporting IDR-mediated LLPS (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the deletion mutant data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Endogenous BMP2K forms cytoplasmic puncta that are eliminated by hexanediol treatment.
claims.source: To determine whether BMP2K could form puncta through LLPS on endogenous expression level, we generated BMP2K 3xHA tag knock-in HeLa cells through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated recombination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I). Successful knock-in was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J). Two types of BMP2K patterns were found, in cytoplasmic puncta or both in cytoplasmic puncta and nuclei (Figure 4F). Nuclear BMP2K was not observed in overexpression expression experiments and could be due to a different isoform. Importantly, cytoplasmic puncta of endogenous BMP2K were also eliminated by Hex treatment (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the knock-in cell data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: KA recorded 22 kinases with some level of mitochondrial localization.
claims.source: KA recorded 22 kinases with some level of mitochondrial localization (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: 14 of the 22 mitochondrial kinases have been documented in mitochondrial proteome database MitoCarta2.0.
claims.source: 14 of them have been documented in mitochondrial proteome database MitoCarta2.0 (Calvo et al., 2016; Figure 5A), among which 6 were confirmed by co-staining with mitochondrial marker translocase of outer membrane 20 (TOM20) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with MitoCarta2.0 database and citation to Calvo et al., 2016.

claims.source: It was reported that FASTK transcribed from an alternative start codon missing N-terminal 34 amino acids was mitochondrial (Jourdain et al., 2015), which we could confirm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to Jourdain et al., 2015.

claims.claim: KA found eight new mitochondrial kinases.
claims.source: Remarkably, we found eight new mitochondrial kinases, which were confirmed by co-staining with TOM20 (Figure 5A, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the co-staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: KA revealed five new mitochondrial kinases: MOK, LIMK2, PKN3, PRKCH, and TNK1.
claims.source: Taken together, KA revealed five new mitochondrial kinases, MOK, LIMK2, PKN3, PRKCH, and TNK1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings after comparison with databases.

claims.claim: Endogenous MOK is present in mitochondria.

W: whole cell lysate; N: nucleus; MI: mitochondria; C: cytosol. Lamin A/C, MT-CO2, and Actin are nuclear, mitochondrial, and cytosolic markers, respectively. Equal loading was achieved by normalizing to the same number of cells. Arrowheads indicate MOK (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: MOK, TNK1, and RPS6KA6 signals were wrapped around by TOM20, indicating transportation into mitochondria.
claims.source: Using 3D structured illumination microscopy (3D-SIM), we found that signals of MOK, TNK1, and RPS6KA6 were wrapped around by TOM20, an OMM protein (Figure 6A), indicating transportation into mitochondria.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the 3D-SIM data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: LIMK2 was in puncta partially colocalizing with TOM20, indicating that LIMK2 decorated the outer surface of mitochondria.
claims.source: In contrast, LIMK2 was in puncta partially colocalizing with TOM20, indicating that LIMK2 decorated the outer surface of mitochondria.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the 3D-SIM data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: MOK2 is imported into mitochondria.
claims.source: MOK2 is imported into mitochondria. Transfected HeLa cells were fixed and permeabilized with digitonin or Triton X-100 before staining.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the differential permeabilization data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: MOK is not a mitochondrial membrane protein.
claims.source: MOK is not a mitochondrial membrane protein. Mitochondria purified from transfected HeLa cells were incubated in indicated buffers, and then centrifuged. Supernatants (S) and pellets (P) were analyzed by western blotting. Equal loading was achieved by normalizing to the same number of cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the extraction data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: MOK is an IMS protein.
claims.source: MOK is an IMS protein. COS-7 cells transfected with MOK2-GFP were imaged by Hessian SIM. MitoTracker Red marked inner membrane (IMM) and co-transfected HSP60-mCherry marked matrix.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including permeabilization, extraction, and super-resolution imaging shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claims.claim: MOK2 has better mitochondrial localization than MOK1.

claims.evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Two peptides 53–103 and 301–330 of MOK2 mediated the mitochondrial localization of MOK.
claims.source: Therefore, two peptides 53–103 and 301–330 of MOK2 mediated the mitochondrial localization of MOK (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the deletion mutant analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of TOM20 but not TOM70 blocked mitochondrial localization of MOK.

claims.evidence: This is supported by the knockdown data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Knockdown of TIM23, TIM17A, and TIM50 eliminated mitochondrial MOK.

claims.evidence: This is supported by the knockdown data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.source: Knockdown of HSPA9, which is responsible for translocation of matrix protein downstream of the TIM23 complex, also suppressed MOK mitochondrial localization (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the knockdown data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The number of cristae markedly reduced in MOK KO cells.
claims.source: Electron microscopy revealed that while mitochondria length remained normal, the number of cristae markedly reduced in MOK KO cells (Figure 7A, B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claims.claim: The cristae defect in MOK KO cells could be rescued by re-expression of MOK1 or MOK2.
claims.source: This defect could be rescued by re-expression of MOK1 or MOK2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Oxygen consumption rates for both basal respiration and ATP production were reduced in MOK KO cells.
claims.source: Cristae have a pivotal role in generating ATP (Cogliati et al., 2013). Indeed, oxygen consumption rates (OCRs) for both basal respiration and ATP production were reduced in MOK KO cells (Figure 7C, D).

claims.claim: Re-expression of MOK2 rescued mitochondrial respiration in MOK KO cells.

claims.source: Consistently, knockout of MOK reduced cellular ATP level, which could be rescued by MOK2, but not MOK1 (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: Oxidative stress induced by diamide caused more apoptosis in MOK KO cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, oxidative stress induced by diamide caused more apoptosis in MOK KO cells (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.source: Using in vitro autophosphorylation as an assay, we confirmed that MOK2 was kinase inactive (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I), consistent with its incomplete kinase domain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claims.source: Nevertheless, MOK2 not only had better mitochondrial localization than MOK1, but also rescued mitochondrial structure and functions in KO cells. Thus, MOK played a functional role in mitochondria in an activity-independent manner.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinase-inactive MOK2 rescued mitochondrial defects.

claims.claim: About 20% of proteins co-purified with MOK were mitochondrial proteins.
claims.source: Mass spectrometry revealed that about 20% of proteins co-purified with MOK were mitochondrial proteins, including mitochondrial ribosomal proteins, solute carriers, oxidative phosphorylation-related proteins, and chaperones (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J).

claims.source: Immunoprecipitation confirmed interactions of MOK with IMM protein ATAD3A and solute carriers SLC25A13 and SLC25A11 (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1K).

results.result: The manuscript provides background on the human kinome, establishing that it comprises 538 kinases encoded by ~2% of the genome, catalyzes protein phosphorylation, and is important for disease and precision medicine.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C12 are well-established facts in the field, supported by appropriate citations to Manning et al., Cohen, Greenman et al., Lahiry et al., Klaeger et al., and Zhang et al. These represent accepted knowledge rather than novel findings of this study.

results.result: The authors constructed a kinome plasmid library of 464 kinases (86.2% coverage) with various epitope tags and positions, expressed them in HeLa cells, and successfully annotated 456 kinases to subcellular compartments.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C13-C18 describe the core methodology and are supported by data in Figures 1A-C and Supplementary files. The library composition, expression levels, and annotation success are clearly documented. This represents a substantial technical achievement.

results.result: KA revealed family-enriched subcellular localizations, with 50.2% of kinases in cytosol, 16.4% in nucleus, and 10.3% on plasma membrane, and specific enrichment patterns for kinase families (e.g., STE in cytosol, CMGC/atypical/CAMK in nucleus, TK/AGC on plasma membrane).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C19-C25 are supported by data in Figures 1E-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D. The family-based enrichment patterns are clearly demonstrated through clustering analysis and kinome tree visualization. This represents a novel systematic finding.

results.result: KA complements existing databases (COMPARTMENTS and HPA) by annotating 18 additional kinases, including 6 first-time annotations, with 74.8% consistency with COMPARTMENTS and 103 unique localizations that are largely unpredictable by computational tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31 are supported by comparison analyses in Figures 2A-H. The Venn diagrams, heatmaps, and prediction analyses clearly demonstrate KA's complementary value. However, the authors acknowledge potential mislocalization due to overexpression/tagging, which is an important caveat.

results.result: KA identified seven kinases with novel plasma membrane localization (RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, NLK, MAPK11, FRK) and confirmed POMK localization to the ER.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C33, C35 are supported by imaging data in Figure 3A and fractionation data in Figure 3B-C. The plasma membrane localizations were validated by cellular fractionation, and ER localization was confirmed by co-staining with SEC61B. These represent novel findings.

results.result: SGK3 was identified as a new exosomal kinase that is secreted via a brefeldin A-insensitive, unconventional pathway and enriched in exosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by imaging (Figure 3D), immunoprecipitation from culture medium (Figure 3E), BFA treatment, and ultracentrifugation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). The evidence converges to support SGK3 as an exosomal kinase, though the functional significance remains to be determined.

results.result: MAP4K3 localizes to tubule-like structures that colocalize with microtubules and ER in LKB1-mutant cells, and this localization is inhibited by LKB1 restoration.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by co-staining data (Figures 3F-G), cell-type comparison (Figure 3H), and LKB1 rescue experiments (Figure 3I). The super-resolution microscopy confirms ER colocalization. The LKB1-dependent regulation is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: KA identified kinases with distinct sub-nuclear patterns, including six kinases enriched at the nuclear periphery and two kinases (CDK13, STK19) localized to nucleoli.
results.evaluation: Claims C46, C47, C49 are supported by imaging data in Figure 4A, high-resolution microscopy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and co-staining with nucleolar marker UTP25 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). These represent novel sub-compartment localizations.

results.result: TRIB3, HIPK2, BMP2K, and CIT form liquid-like condensates that are sensitive to hexanediol, exhibit fusion events, and depend on intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) with prion-like domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 are supported by hexanediol treatment (Figure 4B), time-lapse imaging showing fusion (Figure 4C), sequence analysis (Figure 4D), deletion mutant experiments (Figure 4E), and endogenous BMP2K knock-in validation (Figure 4F). The evidence strongly supports LLPS-mediated condensate formation.

results.result: KA identified five new mitochondrial kinases (MOK, LIMK2, PKN3, PRKCH, TNK1) beyond the 14 documented in MitoCarta2.0, with validation by co-staining and fractionation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C56, C58-C60 are supported by imaging data (Figures 5A, C), comparison with MitoCarta2.0, co-staining with TOM20, and fractionation of endogenous MOK from knock-in cells (Figure 5E). The identification of new mitochondrial kinases is a significant finding.

results.result: MOK is localized to the mitochondrial intermembrane space (IMS), as demonstrated by 3D-SIM showing wrapping by TOM20, differential permeabilization, alkaline extraction, and super-resolution imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by multiple complementary techniques: 3D-SIM (Figure 6A), digitonin/Triton permeabilization (Figure 6B), alkaline carbonate extraction (Figure 6C), and Hessian SIM (Figure 6D). The convergent evidence strongly supports IMS localization.

results.result: MOK is imported into mitochondria via a TOM20-TIM23-dependent mechanism involving two peptide sequences (53-103 and 301-330) but independent of classical mitochondrial targeting signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C72 are supported by isoform comparison (Figure 6E), deletion mapping (Figure 6F), shRNA knockdown of import machinery components (Figure 6G), and co-immunoprecipitation with TOM20/TIM23 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G). The evidence demonstrates a novel import mechanism, though some mechanistic details remain unclear.

results.result: MOK knockout reduces mitochondrial cristae number and impairs mitochondrial respiration and ATP production, with rescue by MOK2 re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are supported by electron microscopy (Figures 7A-B), Seahorse analysis (Figures 7C-D), and ATP measurements (Figure 7E). The rescue experiments demonstrate specificity. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

results.result: MOK knockout increases basal ROS levels and sensitizes cells to oxidative stress-induced apoptosis, with rescue by MOK1 and MOK2 re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by ROS measurements (Figure 7F) and apoptosis assays (Figure 7G). The rescue experiments demonstrate specificity. This extends the functional characterization of MOK beyond cristae and respiration.

results.result: MOK2 is kinase-inactive but rescues mitochondrial defects better than MOK1, indicating that MOK functions in mitochondria in an activity-independent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I) and rescue experiments showing MOK2 rescues cristae, respiration, and ATP levels despite lacking kinase activity. This is a surprising and important mechanistic finding.

results.result: MOK interacts with mitochondrial proteins including ATAD3A, SLC25A13, and SLC25A11, and ATAD3A knockdown phenocopies MOK knockout in reducing cristae number.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by TAP-MS (Figure 7H), co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 7I), and ATAD3A knockdown experiments (Figures 7J-K). The ATAD3A phenocopy supports a functional connection, though the precise mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: The KA dataset shows that 19.1% of kinases have single localization, 72.4% have a specific major localization, and 8.5% are multi-localizing.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 summarize the overall distribution patterns in KA and are supported by the complete dataset in Supplementary file 2. This provides a quantitative overview of kinome localization diversity.

results.result: 38.2% of specific nuclear kinases exhibit uneven localization with puncta of varying sizes under overexpression conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 is a summary observation from the KA imaging data. While supported by the dataset, the authors acknowledge that overexpression may contribute to puncta formation, which is an important caveat for interpretation.

results.result: KA discovered 103 kinase localizations different from existing databases that are largely unpredictable by computational tools, suggesting novel localization mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C30, C31 are supported by database comparisons (Figure 2G) and prediction analyses (Figure 2H). The unpredictability by WoLF PSORT and YLoc suggests these localizations involve non-canonical mechanisms. However, validation at endogenous levels is needed for many of these.
